blocks.text: An optimizer is the algorithm responsible for actually turning a computed gradient into a weight update, and while every optimizer shares this basic job, different optimizers do it in meaningfully different ways, with real consequences for training speed, stability, and memory usage.

This topic covers the most widely used optimizers in fine-tuning today, building from plain gradient descent up to Adam and AdamW, the default choice for the vast majority of modern fine-tuning projects.

Once a gradient has been computed, indicating which direction would reduce the loss, the optimizer decides exactly how to translate that gradient into an actual change to the weights, a decision that sounds simple but has been refined considerably through years of research into faster, more stable training.
2. Plain Gradient Descent, The Starting Point

blocks.alt: Plain Gradient Descent, The Starting Point

blocks.text: The simplest possible optimizer just moves the weights a small step directly in the direction the gradient indicates, scaled by the learning rate, a straightforward approach that works but tends to be slow and can struggle with certain loss landscape shapes.

code.content:
# Plain gradient descent, the simplest optimizer
weight = weight - learning_rate * gradient

blocks.text: Momentum improves on plain gradient descent by keeping a running average of past update directions, smoothing out the trajectory and helping training move through flat or noisy regions of the loss landscape more efficiently than reacting purely to the current gradient alone.

Adam combines the momentum idea with an additional adaptive mechanism, automatically adjusting the effective learning rate separately for each individual parameter based on how that parameter gradients have behaved recently, making it robust and fast converging across a wide range of tasks without needing extensive manual tuning.

AdamW is a small but meaningful correction to Adam, fixing how weight decay, covered in more depth as its own topic in this module, interacts with the adaptive learning rate mechanism, and it has become the default optimizer for the vast majority of modern fine-tuning workflows precisely because of this cleaner behavior.

blocks.text: Adam and AdamW both maintain additional per parameter state beyond the weight itself, tracking running estimates used for the adaptive rate mechanism, which means the optimizer itself consumes extra memory proportional to the number of trainable parameters, on top of the memory the weights and gradients already use.

blocks.title: This connects directly to the earlier PEFT discussion
blocks.content: Because optimizer state memory scales with the number of trainable parameters, PEFT methods like LoRA, which train far fewer parameters than full fine-tuning, also dramatically reduce optimizer state memory as a side benefit.

blocks.text: For nearly all fine-tuning projects covered in this course, AdamW is a reasonable, well tested default choice, and most teams do not need to experiment extensively with alternative optimizers unless they encounter a specific training stability or performance issue that AdamW does not resolve on its own.

Beyond learning rate, Adam and AdamW have a small number of additional hyperparameters controlling how aggressively the momentum and adaptive rate mechanisms respond to recent gradients, though the commonly used default values for these settings work well across a wide range of tasks and rarely need adjustment for typical fine-tuning work.

When fine-tuning with a PEFT method like LoRA, covered in the earlier module, the optimizer only needs to maintain state for the small number of trainable LoRA parameters, not the entire frozen base model, meaning optimizer memory overhead is far less of a practical concern than it would be for full fine-tuning of every model weight.

A team fine-tuning with LoRA uses AdamW as their optimizer, the standard default, and finds training proceeds smoothly with well behaved loss curves using the commonly recommended default hyperparameter values, without needing any specialized optimizer tuning.

Because they are training only the small LoRA matrices rather than the full model, the additional memory AdamW optimizer state requires stays modest, confirming that PEFT methods reduce not just the trainable parameter count itself but also this associated optimizer memory overhead.

items: Choosing an unusual or exotic optimizer without a clear reason, when AdamW handles most fine-tuning tasks well by default
Forgetting that optimizer state adds meaningful memory overhead proportional to the number of trainable parameters
Confusing Adam and AdamW, missing the specific weight decay correction that makes AdamW the more common modern default
Spending excessive time tuning rarely adjusted optimizer hyperparameters instead of focusing on learning rate and rank, which usually matter more

blocks.text: In your own words, explain why an optimizer that adapts its effective learning rate per parameter, like Adam, might converge faster than plain gradient descent, which applies the exact same learning rate to every parameter regardless of that parameter own gradient behavior.

An optimizer determines exactly how a computed gradient gets translated into an actual weight update, and AdamW, which builds momentum and adaptive per-parameter rates on top of plain gradient descent while correctly handling weight decay, has become the well tested default choice for the vast majority of modern fine-tuning projects.
